title: Fixed Windows and Two Heaps
focus: The counting window, the streaming median, and the two graph algorithms that come out of Tarjan's low-link idea.

cards.title: Fixed Sliding Window
patterns: Match count instead of dict compare
cards.trigger: Every window of exactly size k, and a question about its contents.
cards.recall: Write the anagram finder from memory. Then answer the efficiency question: comparing two Counters each step is O(26). What is the trick that makes each step O(1)?
useWhen: Find all anagrams of a pattern in a string
Permutation in a string
Maximum or average of every window of size k
Count windows with a given property
Repeated DNA sequences of fixed length

# remove the left edge once the window is oversized
if j >= 0 and s[j] in need:

problem.name: Find All Anagrams in a String

keyInsights: Tracking a `missing` counter of unsatisfied characters makes each step O(1) instead of O(alphabet)
The increment guard `if need[ch] == 0: missing += 1` must run BEFORE the increment, or the bookkeeping drifts
Fixed window means no while loop. One add and one conditional remove per step, always
cards.trap: 'The alphabet is Unicode, not 26 letters.' Fixed-size arrays are out and the O(26) compare argument collapses. The missing-counter version still works, which is why you learn it.

cards.title: Two Heaps
patterns: Max-heap low half, min-heap high half
Rebalance to differ by at most one
cards.trigger: A running median, or any query about the middle of a growing stream.
cards.recall: Write the median stream from memory. Then answer: what invariant links the two heaps, and why do you always push to one heap and then transfer rather than choosing which heap to push to?
useWhen: Find the median from a data stream
Sliding window median, plus lazy deletion
IPO style problems, capital in one heap, profits in the other
Balance two sides of a partition dynamically
Any 'middle element under insertion' query
template: if len(self.hi) > len(self.lo):                      # keep lo >= hi
keyInsights: Invariant: every element in `lo` is at most every element in `hi`, and `len(lo) - len(hi)` is 0 or 1
Push-then-transfer makes the code branchless and correct by construction. Choosing a target heap needs comparisons and gets it wrong
Python has only min-heaps, so `lo` stores negated values. Negate on the way in and on the way out
cards.trap: 'Now it is a sliding window median, so elements leave too.' Heaps cannot delete from the middle. You need lazy deletion with a removal counter, or a sorted container. Say which and why.

cards.title: Side Views and Column Order
patterns: DFS right-first with a depth check
cards.trigger: What you would see looking at the tree from a direction, rather than what is in it.
cards.recall: Write the right side view both ways from memory, BFS and DFS. Then answer: in the DFS version, why does visiting right before left plus `len(out) == depth` give the right answer?
useWhen: Right or left side view
Largest value in each row
Vertical order traversal, group by column index
Bottom view or top view of a tree
Boundary traversal of a tree
template: # BFS: the last node popped on each level
if i == size - 1:                      # last of this level
# DFS: visit right first, and record the first node seen at each new depth
if depth == len(out):        # first time we reach this depth
# Vertical order: BFS carrying (node, col), bucket by col, sort keys at the end
keyInsights: `depth == len(out)` is a neat first-visit test: the output length is exactly the number of depths already recorded
Right-first DFS reaches the rightmost node of every depth before any other node at that depth
Vertical order needs a tie-break rule when two nodes share a column and a row. Ask what it is before coding
cards.trap: 'Vertical order, ties broken by value.' That extra rule forces a sort within each cell and changes the complexity. Do not assume BFS order is the tie-break.

Count subsets with a given sum
Partition into two subsets with a minimum difference

keyInsights: The whole problem is the algebraic transform. Once you have `want`, it is a knapsack you already know
The parity check is not defensive coding, it is a real impossibility case that the tests cover

cards.title: Bridges and Articulation Points
cards.trigger: Which single edge or single node, if removed, disconnects the graph.
cards.recall: Write Tarjan's bridge finder from memory. Then answer the definition that drives everything: what exactly is `low[u]`, and why does strict greater-than mark a bridge while greater-or-equal marks an articulation point?
useWhen: Critical connections, single points of failure
Bridges in an undirected graph
Articulation points, cut vertices
Network resilience and redundancy analysis
Preprocessing before 2-edge-connected component work
template: low  = [0] * n           # lowest disc reachable from this subtree via one back edge
if v == parent: continue           # do not re-cross the tree edge
if low[v] > disc[u]:           # v cannot reach u or above without this edge
low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v])  # back edge: use disc, not low
keyInsights: `low[u]` is the earliest discovery time reachable from u's subtree using at most one back edge. Say that sentence before you code
Bridges use strict `>`. Articulation points use `>=`, plus a special rule for the root, which is a cut vertex only with two or more DFS children
On a back edge you take `disc[v]`, not `low[v]`. Using low there is a subtle and very common bug
cards.trap: 'Parallel edges between the same pair.' Skipping by parent id is then wrong, you must skip by edge id. Real infrastructure graphs have parallel edges, so they will ask.
